site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: A Friend's Quiet Grace
body: In Dvaraka, Krishna welcomed his childhood friend Sudama with bright eyes and an open embrace. Though Sudama arrived in worn clothes with only a small bundle of beaten rice, Krishna seated him with honor as though greeting royalty.

With simple joy, Krishna himself ate the humble offering of chivda from his friend's palm, cherishing the gift more than any treasure. Sudama, shy and content, never once spoke a word of asking for wealth or comfort.

When Sudama returned to his humble home, he found it transformed into a place of plenty by his friend's quiet grace. The thatched hut now shone, and his wife wept softly with gratitude for Krishna's unseen, loving kindness.

stories.title: A Saint's Bowl of Ghee
body: One morning the beloved Varkari saint Namdev prepared fresh bread as an offering, laying it out with quiet devotion. Before he could present it, a hungry dog darted in, seized the loaf, and raced away across the dusty ground.

Namdev did not scold the creature or chase it in anger. Instead he lifted a small bowl of golden clarified butter and followed the dog, calling kindly after it to wait, so the stolen bread would not turn dry in its mouth. To him, the runaway animal was no thief but a guest, a living form of the divine.

The simple chase became a quiet pilgrimage of mercy, the saint's ghee offered as lovingly as if placed before a god. In that ordinary moment, Namdev's hospitality widened to embrace every creature, and what began as loss softened into worship.

stories.title: The King Who Saw the Quiet Lake
stories.source: Nalapana Jataka, The Jataka, vol. I, E. B. Cowell edition (public domain)
body: Far from the shade of their familiar trees, a troop of monkeys wandered under the hot sun, led by their wise Bodhisatta king. When they reached a still lake glinting between the reeds, the thirsty band surged forward with glad cries, for at last there was water to drink.

But the Bodhisatta stayed back, studying the sandy rim. He saw tracks leading down to the lake and none returning, and understood that a water-ogre waited beneath, ready to seize whatever creature entered. Calling his troop to him, he told them to cut hollow reeds and drink from the bank, never stepping into the water itself.

Patiently, one by one, the monkeys sipped the cool water through the slender reeds while the ogre fumed below, unable to reach a single soul. Refreshed and unharmed, the whole troop moved on together, led by a king whose gentle watchfulness had saved them all.

stories.title: The Monkey's Gentle Escape
stories.source: Jataka Tales — Ellen C. Babbitt (1912), Project Gutenberg
body: High on a rose-apple tree that leaned over a slow river, a clever monkey shared his sweet fruit with a passing crocodile, and their friendship ripened with each visit. The crocodile returned often, content beneath the rustling branches.

But the crocodile's wife fell ill and craved the monkey's heart as a cure, so her husband agreed to carry his friend across the water and betray him. When the trap was revealed, the monkey only smiled and said his heart still rested in the rose-apple tree.

The crocodile turned back, and the monkey leaped lightly onto a familiar branch, safe above the water. From there he spoke gently of how no creature truly leaves its heart behind, then kept a wise distance from his faithless friend, grateful for his own bright, quiet life.

stories.title: Arjuna Earns Shiva's Blessing
stories.source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
body: In the snowy Himalayas, Arjuna undertook fierce austerities, seeking divine weapons for the struggles ahead. A great boar rushed at him, and at the same moment a hunter loosed an arrow. Both struck the boar, and a quarrel over the kill broke into combat. To his astonishment, Arjuna found the stranger's strength far beyond his own, as though he wrestled with the mountain itself.

When Arjuna placed offerings at a linga and saw his sacred garland drift onto the hunter, he understood who stood before him. His heart bowed in glad recognition, for the hunter was Shiva, pleased by his courage and steady devotion. The great god smiled and taught him the wondrous Pashupata weapon, then other deities also granted their armaments.

Arjuna's patient discipline met with divine grace, and he rose from the Himalayas renewed in strength and readiness. What he had sought through long hardship was given freely by heaven, a hopeful sign that sincere effort and unwavering devotion are never left unanswered.
